name: Cameroon
snapshot: Ruled since 1982 by Paul Biya, now in his 90s and declared winner of an eighth term in 2025, while an Anglophone separatist conflict grinds on in the west.
culture: Cameroon calls itself "Africa in miniature" for its range of landscapes and some 250 languages. Makossa and bikutsi music came out of Douala and Yaoundé, and Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa" was sampled by Michael Jackson. The Indomitable Lions' run to the 1990 World Cup quarter-finals, led by Roger Milla, remains a national touchstone, as do football-mad cities like Douala.
society: A former German colony split between France and Britain after the First World War, Cameroon is officially bilingual, but the English-speaking minority has long complained of marginalisation. Oil, timber, cocoa and coffee are key exports. Corruption is pervasive, and power has been concentrated in the presidency for decades, with Biya often governing from long stays abroad.
situation: Paul Biya, now 93, was sworn in for an eighth term after the October 2025 election, which officials said he won with about 54 percent; his former minister Issa Tchiroma Bakary claimed victory, and protests were put down with deadly force. Tchiroma, in exile in The Gambia, has campaigned from abroad, including a complaint against Biya under universal jurisdiction in Switzerland, where the president spends long stays, and in October 2026 the authorities suspended his party. On 9 November 2026 Biya called legislative and local elections for 7 February 2027 after two postponements; a vice president, a post restored in April, has yet to be named. The Anglophone conflict in the west and Boko Haram attacks in the Far North continue.
power: A presidential republic in which power is concentrated in the presidency. Biya governs largely by decree and appoints the prime minister and regional officials. Term limits were abolished in 2008.

story: Germany took Kamerun in 1884; after World War One it was split between France and Britain. The French part fought a bloody independence war and became independent in 1960; part of the British side joined in 1961, the root of today's Anglophone crisis. Ahmadou Ahidjo ruled for 22 years, then handed over in 1982 to Paul Biya, who is still president, making him the world's oldest head of state.
